papers.title: Prognostic impact of severe neutropenia in colorectal cancer patients treated with TAS-102 and bevacizumab, addressing immortal-time bias.
papers.one_line: Finds severe neutropenia associated with longer survival after correcting for immortal time, with landmark hazard ratios of 0.30, 0.65, 0.39 and 0.41 across four landmark times.
papers.what_was_done: Severe neutropenia during trifluridine-tipiracil has been linked to longer survival, but some of those studies did not handle the fact that a toxicity occurring during treatment requires surviving to experience it. This single-center retrospective cohort of colorectal cancer patients receiving bevacizumab with trifluridine-tipiracil compared overall survival between those developing grade 3 or worse neutropenia and those not, using two corrections, time-varying Cox regression and landmark analysis. Median overall survival was 15.3 months with severe neutropenia against 10.0 without. In the time-varying model the onset of grade 3 or worse neutropenia was significantly associated with longer survival after adjustment for age and the modified Glasgow Prognostic Score. Landmark analyses at 30, 60, 90 and 120 days gave hazard ratios of 0.30 with an interval of 0.10 to 0.90, 0.65 with 0.30 to 1.42, 0.39 with 0.17 to 0.90, and 0.41 with 0.18 to 0.95. Patients with severe neutropenia received lower relative dose intensity because of dose reductions but had higher disease control rates, and the paper reads neutropenia as a possible indirect measure of adequate exposure, noting that dosing by body surface area alone ignores individual metabolism. Two prior studies of the same question either did not adjust for confounders or did not handle the time-varying nature of the toxicity.

future_research.gap: Whether myelosuppression causes the antitumor effect or is a consequence of adequate dosing is unresolved.
future_research.quote: In particular, it is yet to be established whether myelosuppression enhances antitumor activity by suppressing tumor-promoting cells, such as TAM, or whether severe neutropenia develops as a consequence of administering an optimal dose of TAS-102.

problems.evidence: Four landmark times were used and the results are not stable across them: 30 days gives 0.30, 60 days gives 0.65 with an interval crossing one, and 90 and 120 days give about 0.40. The paper reports all four and reads them as consistent with the time-varying model. Nothing selects among the landmarks, and a study reporting only the 60-day analysis would have concluded there was no association.
problems.quote: Additionally, 30-, 60-, 90-, and 120-day landmark analysis showed that grade ≥ 3 neutropenia was associated with longer survival after adjustment for age and modified Glasgow Prognostic Score, with respective HRs of 0.30 [0.10–0.90], 0.65 [0.30–1.42], 0.39 [0.17–0.90], and 0.41 [0.18–0.95].

problems.evidence: The exposure is a toxicity that leads to dose reduction, so the neutropenic group received less drug and did better, which the paper interprets as neutropenia marking adequate exposure. Correcting the timing leaves an exposure that is simultaneously an effect of the treatment, a marker of how much treatment was absorbed, and a cause of subsequent dose changes, and the analysis adjusts for age and a prognostic score only.
problems.quote: In our study, patients with severe neutropenia exhibited significantly lower relative dose intensity for TAS-102 due to dose reductions in response to severe neutropenia.

papers.title: Preventing immortal time bias in observational studies: a matter of design.
papers.one_line: Letter answering a claim that prospective intention-to-treat design is the only way to avoid immortal time, by setting out cloning and censoring, time-dependent exposure and landmark analysis, and noting that these target different questions.
papers.what_was_done: Responding to a commentary arguing that a prospective intention-to-treat design is the only practical way to detect and avoid immortal time bias in cardiac surgery research, this letter sets out the cause and the alternatives. The cause is stated compactly: at time zero, treatment status should be determined and eligibility met for everyone, time zero should be the same across arms, for example the day of diagnosis, and using future information to assign treatment status at time zero produces the bias because participants must survive to receive the future treatment. Where a clinical decision between two strategies is made at time zero, such as early against late surgery, comparing the intended strategies is not affected, provided follow-up starts at time zero for everyone and patients are analyzed by the decision made; that is an intention-to-treat comparison in an observational study. For the per-protocol effect the letter describes cloning and censoring, where each patient is copied, each copy assigned a strategy at time zero, followed until it deviates and then censored, so a late-surgery clone that never reaches surgery still contributes follow-up. For comparing surgery against medical treatment it describes analysis with treatment as a time-dependent variable and landmark analysis. It closes by noting that these methods answer different research questions.

problems.evidence: The letter's closing point is that the available remedies for one design flaw target different research questions, so choosing among them chooses the estimand. An intention-to-treat comparison of intended strategies, a cloned per-protocol comparison, a time-dependent analysis and a landmark analysis produce four different quantities from one dataset, and the reported output in each case is a hazard ratio with the method named in the statistical section.
problems.quote: Various methods beyond intention-to-treat designs exist to estimate valid treatment effects, even in retrospective studies, however, these methods target different research questions.

problems.evidence: The letter identifies the condition under which the timing problem disappears rather than needing correction: if a clinical decision between the strategies is made at time zero, then the intended strategies can be compared directly, provided everyone's follow-up starts there. That converts the question from how to fix immortal time into whether the decision point is observable, which is a design criterion rather than an analytic parameter. It does not help where the strategies remain indistinguishable at the decision point, which is the case cloning exists for.
problems.quote: If, however, at time-zero a clinical decision is made between two strategies (e.g. early vs. late surgery), a comparison between those intended strategies is not hampered by ITB.

papers.title: On the estimation of the effect of weight change on a health outcome using observational data, by utilising the target trial emulation framework.
papers.one_line: Uses target trial emulation to settle when time zero should be and which confounders should be adjusted when the exposure is weight change measured between two visits, and concludes the exposure remains ill defined and immortal time remains.
papers.what_was_done: When the exposure is change in weight between enrolment and a first follow-up, two questions arise before any analysis: whether baseline is the enrolment date or the first follow-up, and whether confounders should be taken from one or the other. The paper works the problem through a hypothetical trial in which overweight adults aged 45 to 60 free of chronic disease are randomized to high physical activity with low caloric intake, expected to produce weight loss, or high physical activity with standard intake, expected to produce no change, over two years, with permission to abandon the intervention on developing a chronic condition and 18 further years of follow-up for cardiovascular disease. In the constructed data there is no difference between the arms. The same people are then analyzed as a healthcare database in which diet is unrecorded, so the analysis becomes one of a proxy intervention, weight change, rather than of diet and activity. Three methods used in the literature are applied and their biases traced with directed acyclic graphs, and a simulation follows. The recommendation is to adjust for, or exclude on, confounders measured at both baseline and the first follow-up. Two problems are stated as remaining: the exposure is not well defined because there are different ways of changing weight, mitigated only by excluding those who develop a chronic disease, and immortal time bias, which may be small if the interval to first follow-up is short.

future_research.gap: Weight change is a proxy for an unrecorded intervention on diet and activity, and the substitution is made because the data force it rather than because the proxy is well defined.
future_research.quote: That being the case, we now focus on the effect of a ‘proxy intervention’ [ 19 ], i.e. ‘healthy’ weight change from enrolment to the 1st follow-up after two years instead of the effect of physical activity and diet.
future_research.locator: The same dataset from a healthcare database

problems.evidence: After working out the correct baseline and adjustment set, the paper states that the exposure still is not well defined because weight can be changed in many ways with different effects. The only mitigation offered is excluding people who developed a chronic disease, which removes one route to weight loss rather than partitioning the remaining routes into a class with a common effect. This is the versions-of-treatment problem surviving a careful protocol specification.
problems.quote: However, two issues remain (i) the exposure is not well-defined as there are different ways of changing weight (however we tried to reduce this problem by excluding individuals who develop a chronic disease); and (ii) immortal time bias, which may be small if the time to first follow up is short.

problems.evidence: An exposure defined as change between two measurements cannot have a time zero that satisfies everything: at enrolment the exposure is not yet observable, and at the first follow-up the interval before it has been survived. The paper's recommendation resolves the confounder question and leaves the timing question with a magnitude argument, that the residual immortal time may be small when the interval is short, rather than a rule.
problems.quote: Unfortunately, these questions can introduce ambiguity to the definition of ‘baseline’, where eligibility criteria determining who is selected into the study should be met, as well as to the choices of confounders that should be controlled for, i.e. from enrolment or the 1st follow-up?

papers.title: [Comparing the effectiveness of multiple dynamic treatment strategies using target trial emulation].
papers.one_line: German-language methods article arguing that comparing dynamic treatment strategies in real-world data requires three things together, causal diagrams, target trial emulation with cloning, and g-methods, illustrated by when to start antiretroviral therapy.
papers.what_was_done: Treatment questions in routine care are often dynamic, defined by if-then rules on disease course, side effects or concomitant therapy: when to start, stop, interrupt or modify a therapy, what dosing interval to use, in what order to sequence therapies. Randomized trials for such questions are usually missing because the strategies run longer than a trial's follow-up and would need many arms, and because the cost or ethics forbid them. Decision-analytic models are an alternative but are simplifications limited by the evidence entering them. The article sets out a combined approach for observational data: causal diagrams to identify what must be adjusted, target trial emulation in which all possible dynamic strategies are defined, patient data are cloned and each clone assigned to every arm, with censoring of clones violating their assigned protocol, and g-methods to adjust for the informative censoring that censoring creates. Expected outcomes under each strategy are then simulated and compared. The worked example is when to begin antiretroviral therapy in treatment-naive HIV patients, with strategies defined by CD4 thresholds. The stated conclusion is that dynamic strategies can be compared adequately when the three approaches are combined and the necessary data exist.

problems.evidence: The article's claim is that no one of the three components suffices: a causal diagram without the emulation leaves the timing wrong, the emulation without g-methods leaves the artificial censoring uncorrected, and g-methods without the diagram adjust the wrong set. That is a statement about what a defensible analysis must contain rather than which estimator to pick, and it is asserted from a worked example rather than demonstrated by comparison.
problems.quote: Dynamic treatment strategies can be adequately compared using RWD when three causal approaches are combined, and the necessary data are available. These approaches are (1) causal diagrams, (2) target trial emulation, and (3) statistical g-methods.

problems.evidence: The dynamic questions listed, when to start, stop, interrupt or change a therapy, what dosing interval to use, what sequence to follow, whether to pause between therapies, and when to change dose, are each a family of strategies rather than one, and the article's route is to define all of them explicitly and compare. Which threshold values or intervals constitute the strategies to be compared is set by the analyst, in the worked example by CD4 cutoffs.
problems.quote: Die Target-Trial-Emulierung simuliert eine randomisierte klinische Studie, indem alle möglichen dynamischen Strategien definiert, die Patientendaten kopiert („geklont“) und jede:r Patient:in jedem Behandlungsarm zugewiesen werden.

papers.title: Target trial emulation to assess real-world efficacy in the Epidemiological Strategy and Medical Economics metastatic breast cancer cohort.
papers.one_line: Emulates a breast cancer trial in a national cohort and finds the emulation step, which excludes patients with contraindications and so restores positivity, does the correcting work while the choice of adjustment method barely matters.
papers.what_was_done: The study emulated the E2100 randomized trial comparing first-line paclitaxel alone against paclitaxel with bevacizumab in HER2-negative metastatic breast cancer, using 5,538 patients from the French ESME cohort registered between 2008 and 2020, of whom 3,211 were eligible after emulation. Analysis used stabilized inverse probability of treatment weighting and g-computation, multiple imputation for missing data, and a quantitative bias analysis for unmeasured confounding, with confounders selected from a causal diagram. The emulated estimates favored the combination and were close to the trial's hazard ratio of 0.88, with tighter intervals from the larger sample. The methodological finding is about which step did the work. Emulation removed patients preferentially from the paclitaxel-alone arm, many of whom would never have entered the trial and whose probability of receiving bevacizumab was close to zero, which the paper identifies as a positivity violation that a standard adjusted analysis of the full cohort would have carried. After emulation, balance was achieved by weighting for all covariates except age, and the different adjustment methods changed the estimate only slightly. An earlier analysis of the same cohort using propensity score matching without emulation had given 0.7 with an interval of 0.635 to 0.771. The bias analysis found that only an unmeasured confounder both highly imbalanced and highly correlated with mortality would change the conclusion.

future_research.gap: Negative controls could not be used to check residual confounding because that would require linking the cohort to national health insurance data covering care outside cancer therapy.
future_research.quote: This approach was not tested in our analyses because it requires matching the ESME data to the database from the French national health insurance information system to access data outside cancer therapy in ESME patients ( 46 ).

future_research.gap: Whether the same approach transfers to other treatment settings in this cohort is untested.
future_research.quote: The generalizability of our findings would need further target trial emulations in different treatment settings to test and confirm the robustness of using the same approach within real-life ESME-MBC data.

problems.evidence: The registry entry says positivity is handled by describing weights instead of naming unsupported histories. Here the unsupported patients are named by construction: applying the trial's eligibility criteria removes people with contraindications to bevacizumab, whose treatment probability is effectively zero, and the paper identifies their presence in a conventional adjusted analysis as a positivity violation. It shows that this step, not the choice of estimator, produced the corrected result. What it does not supply is a general diagnostic; the criteria came from an existing trial protocol, which most emulations do not have.
problems.quote: The inclusion of such patients in a standard comparative analysis from observational data leads to biased estimates because the probability of being treated for those patients is actually close to zero, a phenomenon called positivity violation in the causal inference framework.

problems.evidence: The paper runs the comparison the entry says nothing requires: several adjustment techniques on the same emulated cohort, plus the same analyses on the unemulated cohort, and reports which step moved the estimate. Its conclusion is that estimator choice is not decisive once the design is right and the confounder data are adequate, which is a conditional answer to the default-estimator question rather than a general one, established on one question.
problems.quote: By contrast, the choice of the adjustment technique is not decisive if the emulation is carried out correctly and if sufficient data of good quality on confounders are available ( 9 ).

problems.evidence: A quantitative bias analysis is run rather than described, and it is used substantively: the paper identifies what an unmeasured confounder would have to look like to overturn the result, then checks two candidates, uncontrolled hypertension and prior deep thrombosis, against population data on their prevalence. That is a bias analysis integrated into the reporting. Negative controls, the other half of the entry's requirement, were unavailable because they need a data linkage the study did not have.
problems.quote: The QBA analyses showed that only an unmeasured confounder that would be highly imbalanced between the treatment arms and highly correlated with mortality would change the values of our treatment estimates.

problems.evidence: The emulation is read against a specific trial whose protocol supplied the eligibility criteria and treatment strategies, and the paper states which components were emulated satisfactorily and where minor exceptions remained. That is closer to a calibrated comparison than a replication verdict, since the alignment is itemized rather than assumed, and it also reports the discrepancy against an earlier analysis of the same cohort with an explanation grounded in the design difference.
problems.quote: In addition, it was possible to satisfactorily emulate critical components of the E2100 RCT protocol, including treatment strategies and inclusion and exclusion criteria, with minor exceptions for rare features not exactly emulated owing to differences in

papers.title: Positive Impact of [18F]FDG-PET/CT on Mortality in Patients With Staphylococcus aureus Bacteremia Explained by Immortal Time Bias.
papers.one_line: Re-examines the reported mortality benefit of imaging in Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia in a prospective seven-hospital cohort with the scan as a time-varying covariate, and finds no association with 90-day mortality.
papers.what_was_done: Several studies reported that positron emission tomography guided management reduces mortality in Staphylococcus aureus bacteremia, with adjusted odds ratios of 0.28 and 0.41 for three-month mortality, effects the paper calls implausibly large for a diagnostic test that can act only through a subsequent intervention. A systematic review had judged all five available studies at severe or moderate risk of bias from confounding by indication and immortal time. This analysis used the prospective IDISA cohort across two university and five non-university Dutch hospitals, enrolling consecutive adults with a positive blood culture from August 2017 to September 2019, excluding those dying within 48 hours since the scan would not be feasible. The scan was performed at the treating physician's discretion. It was modelled as a time-varying covariate, so everyone contributes to the unscanned group until they are scanned, with no lag time, adjusting for age, Charlson comorbidity index, positive follow-up cultures at 48 hours, septic shock and endocarditis, all time-fixed. For infection-related mortality the competing risk was handled by computing the cause-specific hazard ratio and approximating the subdistribution hazard ratio by assigning competing events the maximum follow-up time, because a Fine and Gray model with a time-varying covariate yields subdistribution hazard ratios that are hard to interpret. After correction there was no association with either 90-day all-cause or infection-related mortality.

future_research.gap: A Fine and Gray model with a time-varying covariate produces subdistribution hazard ratios that are difficult to interpret, so the competing risk had to be handled by an approximation.
future_research.quote: However, Fine and Gray models with a time varying covariate result in sub-distribution hazard ratios (HR) that are difficult to interpret [ 19 ].

problems.evidence: A diagnostic test cannot be received by someone who has already died, so the interval from bacteremia to imaging is immortal, and correcting for it removes an apparently large mortality benefit entirely. The paper's prior argument is worth noting: the reported odds ratios of 0.28 and 0.41 were implausible on mechanistic grounds before any analysis, since a scan acts only through what is done with the result, and the design flaw is what made them attainable.
problems.quote: Immortal time bias might be especially important in studies examining the effect of [18F]FDG-PET/CT on mortality, as patients who did undergo [18F]FDG-PET/CT lived long enough to undergo the procedure.

problems.evidence: The estimand for the secondary outcome had to be improvised: the standard competing-risk model gives an uninterpretable quantity when combined with a time-varying exposure, so the analysis reports a cause-specific hazard ratio and approximates a subdistribution hazard ratio by assigning competing deaths the maximum follow-up time. Two design requirements, handling the timing and handling the competing event, cannot be met by any off-the-shelf estimator here.
problems.quote: Therefore, we calculated the cause-specific HR as normal and estimated the subdistribution hazard ratio (sHR) by modeling all patients with a competing event as having reached the maximum follow-up time without having had the event of interest (infection-related mortality).

problems.evidence: Imaging was ordered at the treating physician's discretion, so the decision tracks clinical suspicion of metastatic infection, which predicts mortality. The adjustment set is five prognostic variables entered as time-fixed covariates chosen from a prior analysis of the same cohort, with no stepwise selection and no negative control or bias analysis to bound what remains.
problems.quote: [18F]FDG-PET/CT was available at all hospitals and was performed at the discretion of the treating physician but was not a mandatory procedure in the work-up of SAB.

papers.title: The influence of immortal time bias in observational studies examining associations of antifibrotic therapy with survival in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis: A simulation study.
papers.one_line: Detects immortal time bias in 14 of 16 published studies of antifibrotics in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis and simulates what four handling methods give, from a hazard ratio of 0.55 under a time-fixed analysis to 0.93 under a time-dependent one.
papers.what_was_done: An immortal time bias checklist was applied to observational studies of antifibrotic therapy and survival in idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis, detecting the bias in 14 of 16 studies with insufficient data to judge the other two. A simulation then compared four handling methods on generated data: the time-fixed method gave a hazard ratio of 0.55 with an interval of 0.47 to 0.64, exclusion gave 0.79 with 0.67 to 0.92, the one-year landmark gave 0.69 with 0.58 to 0.81, and the time-dependent method gave 0.93 with 0.79 to 1.09. The time-fixed and exclusion methods therefore overstated effectiveness by 41 and 15 percent relative to the time-dependent method, which the paper treats as closest to the truth, matching an earlier real-data comparison in chronic obstructive pulmonary disease where the same three methods gave 0.55, 0.66 and 0.97. The paper notes that the bias can reverse a result, citing a statin and diabetes progression study where 0.74 became 1.97 after correction. It observes that immediate separation of survival curves at the start of follow-up is a visual signature of the bias, recommends the prevalent new-user design and longer observation periods, and states that landmark performance depends heavily on the timepoint chosen, so multiple landmarks are usually set. Stata code is published.

future_research.gap: The simulation establishes the direction of the bias but not its real magnitude in this literature, which would need linkage to prescription data.
future_research.quote: Future studies should quantify the effect size estimates of the influence of ITB on associations between antifibrotic therapy and survival in patients with IPF based on data linkage with filling of prescriptions, although it could be challenging for getting the data required for such analyses.

problems.evidence: Four accepted handling methods applied to one simulated truth give hazard ratios of 0.55, 0.79, 0.69 and 0.93, spanning most of the range between a large effect and none. The landmark result sits between the biased and unbiased extremes and its position depends on the timepoint chosen, so the reported estimate is a function of a method choice that no reader can undo. The same ordering is reproduced from a real-data comparison in a different disease.
problems.quote: Our simulation study showed that use of time–fixed and exclusion methods overestimated the effectiveness of antifibrotic therapy in reducing the risk of all–cause mortality by 41 and 15%, respectively, compared to the time–dependent method.

problems.evidence: Fourteen of sixteen studies in this clinical area carry the bias, and the two exceptions could not be assessed for want of reported information. The paper notes the bias can reverse an estimate, giving a case where a hazard ratio of 0.74 became 1.97 on correction in the same dataset, so the direction as well as the magnitude of a published conclusion can be an artifact of when follow-up started.
problems.quote: ITB may also on some occasions lead to a reversal of the true effect estimate of interventions.
problems.locator: The importance of addressing ITB in IPF studies

problems.evidence: The landmark remedy excludes everyone who died before the landmark, which the paper flags as most damaging precisely where events cluster early, as they do in this disease. So the correction that is easiest to apply removes the person-time that carries the information, and the paper's alternative recommendation, a longer observation period to dilute the immortal fraction, is unavailable in rapidly progressive disease.
problems.quote: In addition, use of landmark method has a key limitation: subjects are excluded from the analysis which reduces statistical power; this is particularly important in critical care research where events are usually more common early in the disease process in subjects with severe diseases such as IPF.

papers.title: Response to letter entitled: Tixagevimab/cilgavimab pre-exposure prophylaxis and breakthrough infection risk in vaccinated solid organ transplant recipients: Concern for immortal time bias effect.
papers.one_line: Reply establishing that the criticized study had in fact used prescription time-distribution matching, while acknowledging that neither the method's name nor its purpose appeared in the original manuscript.
papers.what_was_done: The authors reply to a letter alleging immortal time bias in their study of antibody prophylaxis in vaccinated solid organ transplant recipients. They accept the concept and give the standard inhaled glucocorticoid example, then argue the bias is unlikely to have affected their result for four reasons. First, follow-up for each vaccine-matched control began on the same day their counterpart in the treated group received the drug, which is prescription time-distribution matching, so any infection in a control before the matched start date does not count as a breakthrough event. They acknowledge that the method was described in their methods without being named and without its bias-reducing role being discussed. Second, prior infection lowers future breakthrough risk and was more common in the control group, which would work against the treated group. Third, review of the 42 controls with prior infection showed that the timing would have precluded treatment for only 3 of the 222 controls at their matched initiation date, which they acknowledge was not in the original manuscript. Fourth, the matching also reduces bias from the varying incidence of infection over calendar time, which is the mechanism the critics had pointed to.

problems.evidence: The exchange happened because a design feature that prevents a named bias was implemented and not labeled. The authors state that the phrase was not used and its association with lower risk of the bias was not discussed, and separately that a count bearing directly on the criticism was not in the manuscript. A reader could not tell from the published report whether the study was vulnerable, which is what a reporting scheme that carried the design decisions and their purposes would fix.
problems.quote: A description of when the follow-up for each participant in the control group is present in the methods, although we acknowledge that the specific phrase “prescription time-distribution matching strategy” was not used and its association with lower risk of immortal time bias was not discussed.

problems.evidence: Prescription time-distribution matching sets each control's start of follow-up to the date their matched treated counterpart received the drug, which aligns the clocks without a landmark and without discarding data, and here also neutralizes calendar-time variation in infection incidence. It works because treatment timing in the treated group supplies the distribution, so it does not extend to designs where the strategies are indistinguishable at the decision point.
problems.quote: This strategy involved starting the follow-up of each vaccine–matched control on the same day that their counterpart in the intervention group received tixagevimab-cilgavimab.

papers.title: The population-attributable fraction for time-to-event data.
papers.one_line: Defines, identifies and estimates the population attributable fraction in time-to-event settings with competing risks and a time-dependent exposure by combining causal inference with multi-state modeling and inverse probability weighting.
papers.what_was_done: The population attributable fraction is often misestimated or misinterpreted, and the risk is highest in time-to-event settings. The paper defines it, gives identification conditions, and estimates it where competing risks and a binary time-dependent exposure are both present, using multi-state methodology with weighted Aalen-Johansen estimators for the two components of the fraction, which reduce to Kaplan-Meier estimators when there are no competing risks. The construction avoids competing risks bias and immortal time bias and reduces confounding from both baseline and time-varying characteristics, and is implemented with standard R packages. Applied to intensive care data, it estimates that 812 deaths, 4.1 percent, in French adult intensive care units in 2016 were preventable had ventilator-associated pneumonia been eliminated, adjusted for age, patient type and a time-dependent organ failure score with bootstrap intervals. The paper works through why interpretation in competing risks settings is hard: in this application the infection had no significant effect on the death rate but reduced the discharge hazard, prolonging hospital stay and thereby raising the risk of in-hospital death, so eliminating it would reduce hospital deaths by increasing discharges. Where the competing risk is itself harmful, eliminating an exposure can produce a negative attributable fraction even though the exposure harms, if it reduces competing events more than events of interest.

future_research.gap: No sensitivity analysis technique has been tailored to the time-dependent attributable fraction in the presence of a competing event, although identification needs strong unverifiable assumptions.
future_research.quote:
However, to our knowledge, none of these techniques have so far
been tailored to estimation of the time-dependent PAF in the presence of a competing event.

problems.evidence: The entry says competing events are handled as cleaning rather than as an identifying choice. This treats them as states in a multi-state model, so eliminating the exposure changes the transition hazards to every state, and shows what that means substantively: in the worked example the exposure did not raise the death rate but lowered the discharge rate, and the attributable deaths arise through the longer stay. The construction also removes immortal time and time-varying confounding at once rather than sequentially. The interpretive problem remains, and the paper states it: where the competing event is harmful, a harmful exposure can yield a negative attributable fraction.
problems.quote:
By combining causal inference and multi-state modelling, we maintain
the causal interpretation of the PAF and avoid severe yet common types of biases including
competing risks bias, immortal time bias, and reduce time-varying confounding.

problems.evidence: Identification here needs strong unverifiable assumptions, and the paper points to the general sensitivity analysis literature while stating that none of those techniques has been adapted to this estimand with a competing event. So the setting where several assumptions are doubtful at once, time-varying confounding, competing risks and time-dependent exposure, is precisely the setting with no sensitivity analysis available.
problems.quote:
For identification of the PAF strong unverifiable assumptions for causal inference from
observational data are required.

problems.evidence: A literature review of infectious disease journals is cited as having found fundamental shortcomings in the very conception of attributable mortality, and the paper notes that statisticians took time to agree on a causal quantification of the fraction in these settings. A quantity that has been reported for decades therefore lacked an agreed definition in the data structures where it is most used.
problems.quote:
A literature review of journals on infectious
diseases revealed fundamental shortcomings in the conception of attributable mortality in

papers.title: Tixagevimab/cilgavimab pre-exposure prophylaxis and breakthrough infection risk in vaccinated solid organ transplant recipients: concern for immortal time bias effect.
papers.one_line: Letter arguing that a reported protective effect of antibody prophylaxis in transplant recipients is inflated by immortal time, using the calendar concentration of dosing against the calendar pattern of infection rates.
papers.what_was_done: The letter comments on a study reporting lower COVID-19 breakthrough infection in vaccinated solid organ transplant recipients who received tixagevimab and cilgavimab. It sets out the mechanism: assignment to treated or untreated used information observed after cohort entry, so treated participants were necessarily event free between entry and their first dose and contributed that time to the treated group. It then makes the argument empirically from the reported data rather than in the abstract. Infection rates differed between the early and late periods of data collection, 1.8 percent in the treated group against 6.3 percent in the untreated between January and March, and 3.2 against 8.1 percent between April and May. Of the initial doses, 98.2 percent were given during the early period, and an infection during that period would have precluded receiving the drug. The concentration of dosing in the period with the widest gap in infection rates is the signal the letter reads as immortal time distorting the comparison in favor of the intervention, in particular in the lung transplant subgroup where the treated group had fewer infections.

problems.evidence: The letter shows how a reader can detect the bias from published summary numbers alone: dosing concentrated in one calendar period, an infection in that period precluding treatment, and infection rates differing between periods. That is a diagnostic built from what the paper happened to report, not from anything the reporting convention requires, and it can only raise a concern rather than quantify the distortion.
problems.quote: Of the initial doses of T/C, 98.2% were administered during the early period, and infections occurring during this period would preclude administration of T/C.

papers.title: Commentary: Maintenance with hypomethylating agents after allogeneic stem cell transplantation in acute myeloid leukemia and myelodysplastic syndrome: A systematic review and meta-analysis.
papers.one_line: Commentary arguing that pooling retrospective post-transplant maintenance studies amplifies rather than resolves immortal time bias, since patients dying before the maintenance start date fall into the control arm by default.
papers.what_was_done: A meta-analysis had reported better overall and relapse-free survival, and lower relapse and non-relapse mortality, with hypomethylating agent maintenance after allogeneic transplantation, concluding that maintenance is beneficial. The commentary argues that pooling makes the problem worse rather than better in this setting. Patients receiving maintenance at, say, day 60 after transplant are by construction those who survived to day 60, and patients who died earlier are assigned to the control arm although they were candidates for maintenance, so the interval between transplant and initiation is immortal and the bias attributes benefit to the drug. Four remedies are listed: starting follow-up for both groups at the end of the identified immortal period; comparing two calendar periods with different treatment strategies; treating exposure as a time-dependent variable so patients are unexposed until they meet the exposure criteria; and a nested case-control design. The commentators describe their own study of azacitidine maintenance in 185 patients, 65 treated and 120 control, in which they excluded everyone who died, relapsed or developed grade 2 or worse graft-versus-host disease before day 60 to avoid the bias, used time-to-event methods accounting for censoring and competing risks, and used multivariable Cox and Fine-Gray models, finding no difference in relapse, overall survival or event-free survival. The conclusion is that only a randomized study can settle the question.

future_research.gap: The question is judged unanswerable from the existing retrospective evidence, so a randomized trial is required.
future_research.quote: Because of this limitation, we believe that to assess the benefit of HMA maintenance treatment after allograft, only a randomized study can allow a definitive conclusion.

problems.evidence: Meta-analysis is described as the highest level of evidence and is shown here to inherit rather than average out a shared design flaw: every contributing study places early deaths in the control arm by construction, so pooling tightens the interval around a biased estimate. The commentators' own bias-avoiding analysis of the same clinical question found no difference, so the pooled conclusion and the corrected single study disagree.
problems.quote: Such work may even amplify the bias or misinterpretation involved in many retrospective studies.

problems.evidence: Maintenance therapy after a transplant necessarily starts weeks after the transplant, so every study of it has an immortal interval unless the design removes it. The remedy the commentators used in their own work was to exclude anyone who died, relapsed or developed significant graft-versus-host disease before day 60, which aligns the clocks by discarding the early period and its events, and defines the estimand as an effect among day-60 survivors.
problems.quote: The elapsed time between allo-HCT and HMA initiation is an immortality period during which subjects who were candidate to receive HMA but died prematurely are counted as patients without HMA.

papers.title: A potential outcomes approach to defining and estimating gestational age-specific exposure effects during pregnancy.
papers.one_line: Defines gestational age-specific exposure effects as contrasts in a target trial where delivery can interrupt exposure initiation, and gives weighting, g-computation and targeted maximum likelihood estimators, showing that a standard weighted analysis censoring early deliveries is biased.
papers.what_was_done: Pregnancy exposures are studied observationally, and both when the exposure started and how long it lasted matter, while pregnancy loss or delivery can end follow-up at any point. The paper defines effects relative to a hypothetical randomized trial of timed pregnancy exposures where delivery may precede and interrupt initiation, which fixes a common baseline and entrance criteria and evaluates exposure prospectively rather than grouping participants by a retrospective summary of their pregnancy. Contrasts are defined between strategies that can be adhered to regardless of health or pregnancy outcomes during follow-up, so eligible participants need not be excluded on post-baseline status. Two parameters follow, the effect of initiating treatment at different times and the effect of initiating and sustaining it. Inverse probability weighted, g-computation and targeted maximum likelihood estimators are constructed; because delivery time varies, the nuisance quantities must be decomposed into random and constant components, and only the targeted estimator can formally accommodate nonparametric modeling of them. Simulation shows a standard weighted implementation that censors early deliveries is substantially biased, while an unmeasured confounder of early delivery and the outcome does not affect the proposed estimators. The application evaluates inhaled corticosteroids and birthweight in mild asthma, with all intervals covering the null and point estimates suggesting benefit at 20 weeks largely mediated by delivery time.

future_research.gap: The outcome must be definable at every time delivery or loss can occur, which fails for birthweight in early pregnancy loss, and the three proposed workarounds each have costs.
future_research.quote: An important limitation of the applicability of these methods is that the outcome must be defined and measurable for all time points under study where delivery or pregnancy loss is possible.

future_research.gap: Separating the effect mediated by delivery time from the direct effect would need adjustment for all confounders of delivery time and a method for time-varying exposure and mediator.
future_research.quote: This would, however, require adjustment for all confounders of delivery time and a method that can incorporate time-varying exposures and mediator.

problems.evidence: The entry says nothing outcome-blind selects the timing. Here the timing is built into the estimand: a common baseline, prospective evaluation of exposure status rather than retrospective summarizing, and strategies specified so that they remain followable whatever happens to the pregnancy, which removes the need for post-baseline exclusions. The paper shows what the alternative costs, since a weighted analysis censoring early deliveries is substantially biased. It is specific to a setting where the interrupting event, delivery, is itself the time scale.
problems.quote: The target trials approach avoids immortal time-bias and exposure misclassification by defining a common baseline and entrance criteria and by prospectively evaluating exposure status rather than grouping participants retrospectively according to a summary of their pregnancy exposures.

problems.evidence: Birthweight does not exist for a pregnancy that ends in early loss, so the outcome is undefined rather than unobserved for part of the population. Three routes are named, a composite including no live birth, separable direct and indirect effects decomposing the treatment, and a principal stratum of pregnancies that would always end in live birth, and the paper states that none removes the problem: cohorts restricted past a time threshold are typical and selection bias is omnipresent for early exposure effects.
problems.quote: However, because it is difficult to identify pregnancy initiation and very early pregnancy losses, cohorts restricted to pregnancies that cross a time threshold are typical and selection bias omnipresent for the estimation of early exposure effects during pregnancy,

problems.evidence: Three estimators are supplied for the same parameters and they are not interchangeable: because variable delivery time forces the nuisance quantities to be decomposed, only the targeted maximum likelihood estimator can formally accommodate nonparametric modeling of the components, and even then convergence rate restrictions apply. So the choice of estimator determines what flexibility is available for the nuisance models, in a setting where the correct forms are unknown.
problems.quote: In particular, among these, only TMLE can formally incorporate nonparametric modeling of these components, though some convergence rate restrictions apply.
